title: A Mardi Gras job with a bad band and Johnson Park with Bolden
summary: He tells how he took a Mardi Gras pickup job with a rough band and had to lead on bass, then talks of Johnson Park and playing years with a trumpeter who wrote Funky Butt.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Oh yeah, they're pretty in there. Oh yeah, it's a nice place. And the people, just go there, it was swell. Did they have a bandstand? The old bandstand and everything. Is it up high or down before? No, we had it high enough, you know, so for my bass, because they couldn't have it too low. No. Oh yeah, we had it. We made money there through trips. And first got, got drunk somewhere, they come there, they come there with the cabaret, the buggy. And they come there, we'll be playing, they start to dance. Play that over, play that over. Bam! Four beats, six beats. Yeah. And uh, for the music proposition, I played with uh, one mardi gras, one tether. Y'all can take that too if you want. I was sitting under my step, I was living on San Antonio and said, you know I was living on the other side. And uh, on the mardi gras, I had no job at all, you know, I was going to play, I had no job. I sat on the mardi gras on the day on the truck. I said, you know, people has come there, poor people has come there, I said, no, it's that. And I had a little in them days, you know. I looked, Lenny, what's she doing there? I said, nothing, looking at the mardi gras. And uh, he said, you know, we look for bass player now. We thought about you, we thought you was playing, I said, you know, I'm playing. I said, I must be, you want to play? I said, yeah, I said, I want to play. I thought you could play, you know. I said, what is your pen? Fun for a lot. Oh, I said, I'd go for ten. You know, I'm playing the pen and using the jazz, you know. I said, y'all got the deposit? He said, you hold this nice day. He said, give me ten dollars. I went inside, I picked myself up, I went. Boy, boy, I'm sorry, I picked them ten dollars. He, he, he. He had a guitar, bass, clarinet, and the trumpet. Well, they played up time. I thought you could play all right, you know. Well, it doesn't matter. The rod is bang, man. I've never used my whole life. I got to go to myself, I saw I made a mistake. I watched it on my step. I was like, oh, my God. Up time, you know, I don't know so many people up time, but when they come down here, you know. When they come, they took, you know, all them prayers. They was from down here too, the people. When they took clay, they come in that clay once. I said, Lord, you know what I've done? You know, I always stand up to play my bass. I think. I don't know what I was doing. My cousin told me, I see you in that bad band. That rotten band. I see you in that bad band. Well, when they passed, after they passed clay boy, several last weeks, you know, they went downtown. So, what was wrong when they put in the time, they knock off? The wife, I don't know if I even had the contract. The fellow said, well, who must I pay? Now, he asked, who must he pay? Because the trumpet player had the job, you know. You see, what I'm going to tell you, you see, old man, trust me that old man who didn't have no band at all. That is what I'm saying at the front of myself. I have to play bass, violin and lock. They start a number they couldn't figure. I had to pay. Then he gave me $2 extra. What were you on that day? How did you get around that day? Because my job was their job. Yeah, but I mean, was it a truck or a wagon? A truck. Oh, no truck. And man, when you come, I don't forget that day long as I lived. It's about, oh, it's been the first couple of years now, about four or five years ago, four years ago. So, never take another hand like that. I was, phew, I said, Lord, never no more. Them people surely play some band music. And I have to lead and play bass. Bass is no lead, but bass is no. Tell us about Johnson Park a little. Oh, Johnson Park? I was playing there with a man of Paris, who was playing at Tooth Park next to him. You know about that baseball place, that park thing, you know? That platform, you could dance every Sunday. Man of Paris, he had a band there. And I was playing with, what do I call him again? What? Baldwin? Baldwin. That boy could play some trumpet. You've seen good trumpet player? Yes. He's the one composed Funkabuck, Funkabuck, let me tell them, forgot that. Funkabuck, Funkabuck, David Lawrence. Yes. He composed that. He had a good band too. And he's- How long did you play with him? Oh, I played about two, three years with him. Oh, yes. I played with him long- I was a kid, René. I played five years with him. He used to- He used to come get me to play so much music. My mother couldn't talk French, you know, couldn't talk American. When she come, I'd be some time, I'd be tired, you know, I'd play so much. You see, Mr. Ben is, Albert is there? Yes, he's there. He's a good man. Yes, he's there. So, I said, can I see him? You say yes? Yes, he's a good guy. You know, I said, Albert, I'm not a crew, you know. Albert was going to watch him. Albert was going to watch him. He said, I said, he's going to come in. And he said, he came in. How was you playing tonight? And he's turning the door, right, Mama B? What's the matter? She could say bass, you know. She said, you want to kill my son? That boy ain't got no risk. My God, you want to kill my boy? She's got somebody else who can play bass. She could say bass, you know. Yes. You say, what's the matter? Think I'll play bass, play, and I'll go so much as that. Now he, she's calling, he, she. Oh, yes. He's calling you, she.
